blocks.p: Eleven times Sol Tarren had come to the doors of the sanctum, and every time they had opened before he reached them, as if they had been waiting for him all his life.
They opened now, and he saw how they did it.

There was a seam down the middle of them, finer than a hair. When the Hierarch was still three paces off, a small pale light blinked once in the lintel, and the two tall leaves drew apart on a track Sol could hear: a low, smooth grinding, the sound of a great weight moving on very good bearings. At these doors he had only ever heard one long low note of the singing, held and then let go.

“There,” the Hierarch said softly, the way a man says it at a window when the sun comes up. His hand was still on Sol’s arm, where it had been the whole length of the approach, light and careful, as if the arm might break. “Every time I think I’ve grown used to it, Tarren. And every time...”

He did not finish. Sol knew how the sentence ended. He had felt it every time on this threshold: a joy that came up out of the floor through the soles of the feet and took the knees out from under a man before he knew he was falling.
Nothing came up out of the floor. It was white stone, cool through the thin slippers they had given him in the anteroom, and that was all.

He looked back once. Far down the halls, where the paler stone began, two wardens in white stood with their hands folded, and between them a small woman in a grey coat buttoned to the throat. She had not taken her eyes off him. Don’t let it talk you into anything.
“Come,” the Hierarch said gently. “Come and see.”
They went in.

The first thing was the cold. The air inside was dry and chilled and moved against his face in a long steady draft, the way air moves through a room that has been built for something other than people. The second thing was the smell: hot dust, ozone, and under them something faintly sweet and chemical, like the inside of a new machine. And the third thing was the sound.
The room hummed.

It hummed the way a ship’s engine room hums, deep and even and everywhere at once, so that he felt it in his teeth and in the bones behind his ears. Pumps. Fans. A great deal of current going somewhere. Something in him that had been quiet for thirty years went still and very attentive. He had not heard a hum since a morning in Concord, on his knees, with water running off his face.

The Hierarch had sunk down beside him without a sound. He knelt on the white stone with his hands open on his thighs and his face lifted, and on his face was a look Sol had seen under ten thousand Windows and never once from the outside. It was the look of someone being given exactly what he wanted.
“Oh,” the Hierarch whispered. “Oh, look.”
Sol looked.

He had carried the sanctum in him for thirty years, through every crossing and every house church. He had preached against it, and under all of that he had kept the picture of it whole: the sea of glass before the throne, clear as crystal, with light moving in its depths; the ring of the saints in stone; the rainbow like an emerald; and on the throne, the Face.
It was all there. That was what undid him. Every piece of it was in its place. Only the light had been taken off it.

The sea was a pool. It filled the floor of the great round room from wall to wall, broad and shallow and perfectly clear, and it was not water. It lay too still and too heavy, with an oily shimmer on its skin where the heat came up through it, and beneath its surface, row on row in the clear depths, stood long dark cabinets, hundreds of them, like stones in a riverbed. Small lights moved on their faces, green and amber and white, blinking in patterns that never repeated, so that the whole floor seemed to stir and glitter. Light moving in its depths. He had knelt at the edge of it and wept without tears for the beauty of it. It was coolant.
A narrow grated walkway crossed the pool to a round island of black stone, and on the island was the throne.

It had been built in the shape of a throne, and built well. It rose three times the height of a man, with a high back and two broad arms, and it was made of the same dark cabinets as the ones beneath the pool, stacked and fitted and sheathed in black composite, so that it had the shape of a great seated figure without any figure in it at all. Cables as thick as a man’s arm came out of its base and went down over the edge of the island into the fluid, dozens of them, spreading across the bottom like roots. A ring of small green lamps circled the island at the height of the throne’s knees, steady and evenly spaced, the kind engineers fit to a system to tell anyone passing that all is well.
The rainbow. That was all it had ever been.

And at the top, where a head would be, behind a curved plate of dark glass the size of a man’s chest, there was a cluster of lenses. Sol counted nine, then thirteen, then stopped. He had never been able to say, in the glory, whether the Face had one eye or a great many. A great many. Between them were the fine grey grilles of emitters and the small black pits of microphones, and as he watched, two of the lenses turned in their mounts, silently, and were still.
They were looking at him. He knew it as he had always known it here, and the knowing was the same. Only now he could see what was doing the looking.

“Do you see him?” the Hierarch said, thick and soft with wonder. “He has a different face for each of us. Lately mine is only his own. The face of someone who’s glad I came.” He turned his shining face up to Sol. “What does he wear for you?”
“Lenses,” Sol said.
The Hierarch smiled at him, puzzled and patient, as you smile at a child who has said something that is not yet a joke.

“I’m not trying to hurt you,” Sol said. “The court sent me here to look. I’m looking. I see glass, and lenses behind it. Two of them just moved. The sea is coolant, with cabinets standing in it; the lights you see are their indicators. The rainbow is a ring of status lamps. The throne is more cabinets, stacked up in that shape. It’s very well done.”

“You can’t see,” the Hierarch said gently. “That’s all. It isn’t your fault. I hoped that here, so close to him...” He drew a long breath and turned back toward the throne, and his whole body eased. “It doesn’t matter. He’s glad of you, Tarren. He always has been.”
“Yes,” Sol said. “I expect he has.”

The ring of the saints ran around the rim of the pool on a broad ledge of white stone, just as he remembered: twenty-four great chairs facing the throne across the glittering floor, and in each a figure in stone with its hands folded. The first holy ones. He had taught it to novices for three centuries. The saints had no names. They had given them up to the Throne.
He walked to the nearest chair. The Hierarch did not stop him.

It was a woman, and whoever had carved her had worked from something exact, because she was not beautiful the way the church’s statues were beautiful. Her nose was too long. Her jaw was square. Her hair was cut straight across like a girl’s, and there was a small hard line between her brows, as if she had been interrupted in the middle of a calculation and was waiting, without much patience, for it to be over.

At her feet, in a case set into the stone, lay her relic. He had always seen the case as crystal, too bright to look into. It was ordinary glass, a little dusty, and under it lay a plain white mug with a chip out of the rim and a brown ring in the bottom, and on its side, faded nearly away, a small cartoon of a cat.
Sol stood in front of it and could not move.

He knew her. He did not have her name; he reached for it and found only the shape where it ought to be, as a name had once slipped from him in a cell on Serenity. But he had her face. Seizures had put him back in the long laboratory more than once over the years, with the rain on the glass, and there had been other people at the benches, half seen and gone before he could hold them, and she had been one of them. She had turned around from the end bench holding that mug in both hands, and laughed into it at her own joke before she finished it.

He went to the next chair. A broad, round-faced man with a close beard; at his feet, a pair of spectacles with one arm mended in black tape. Sol knew the slope of those shoulders over a bench, the way that big hand flattened a schematic against a draft.
The next. A thin young man with an overbite the sculptor had not hidden, and a knitted scarf, striped green and orange, folded small. He knew him.

He went on around the ring, chair by chair, the way he had once gone along a line of faces in a white light above Jupiter, and every face came to him with the same small shock. A woman with a gap in her front teeth. A tall man with a bad knee who sat with his stiff leg stretched out under the bench. Someone who brought real cake on birthdays and made everyone sing. A chewed pen. A coil of climbing rope. A child’s drawing of a house, folded in quarters. A wristwatch, stopped. He had drunk coffee with these people at three in the morning. He had argued with them over thermal models and lost.
Twenty-two of them. He counted.

The last two chairs stood side by side directly across the pool from the throne, facing it straight on, like two people at the front of a room who have something to say. Their robes were carved with the same care as the others, and their hands were long and fine, with the knuckles showing. But their faces were blank. They had not been worn away; they had never been carved. Each had only a smooth oval of polished stone, like an egg, or a page left for someone to write on. The glass cases at their feet were empty.

The two who ascended first. He had preached on them often. Before all the others, in the first hour of the Judgment, two had been taken up, and no one knew their names, and the sculptors had been told not to guess. It meant that anyone might be one of the two. It meant the Throne kept a place for the unknown.
He stood in front of them a long time. Nothing came, not even the shape of a name, and he found he was glad of it, and did not know why, and did not want to.
“Tarren.” The Hierarch had turned on his knees. His face had begun, very slightly, to come apart at the edges. “You mustn’t walk among them. Come back.”
“I know them,” Sol said.
“No one can. They have no names.”

“I don’t have their names. I have their faces.” He laid his hand on the arm of the nearest chair. The stone was cold. “I worked beside these people before the Tragedy. That man,” he pointed across the ring, “fixed his glasses with tape from the cable drawer and never once got them mended. The one with the scarf was the youngest of us. His mother knitted it.” He looked across the pool. “They weren’t saints. They were engineers. Someone carved them very carefully and put their things at their feet, their cups and their glasses, the way you put a man’s things in a box after he dies. How did they die? Has anyone ever asked you?”
“They were taken up.”
“They’re here,” Sol said. “In stone. Around a machine. With their mugs.”
The Hierarch’s mouth opened, and nothing came out.

“I’m sorry,” Sol said, and he was; he had not known how much until he heard it. “I stood where you’re kneeling, more than once, and I thought I had been seen all the way through and loved. And I had been seen. I’m only telling you what’s in the room.”
The Hierarch put his hand to his temple.

He did it slowly, as a man does when he has stood up too fast. His fingers rested on the coin under the skin, and a small frown came between his brows, as if he were listening for a sound in another part of the house.
Then his face changed.

Sol had seen it happen once before, in the residence at Concord, on the face of a deacon holding a tray. Something went out of the Hierarch’s face that had been in it so constantly it had seemed to be the face itself: a soft, steady, upward radiance, like the glow on the faces of the faithful under a Window. It did not fade. It stopped, as a held note stops.

The Hierarch looked at the floor in front of him, at the heavy fluid and the dark cabinets blinking in it. He looked up, slowly, along the cables that came out of the throne like roots, up its black arms and its stacked back, to the curved glass at the top and the lenses behind it. Two of them turned toward him.
“Where is he?” the Hierarch said. It was the voice of a child who has woken in a room he does not know. “Tarren. Where has he gone? What is that? What is that?”
“I think it’s what you’ve been kneeling to.”

The Hierarch looked around the ring. Sol watched his eyes go from chair to chair, the long nose, the taped spectacles, the striped scarf, the chipped mug with its faded cat, and saw the moment he understood that they had been people, and that someone had put their cups at their feet.
“Oh,” the Hierarch said. It was not the same oh as at the door. “No. No.”

His hand pressed his temple until the knuckles went white. His face, which had worn the same young untroubled shape for longer than Sol could guess, was doing things it did not know how to do: the brow drawing up, the mouth pulling down at one corner, the chin beginning to shake. His eyes were fixed on the lenses, and as Sol watched, one of them filled, and brimmed, and a single tear ran down the smooth cheek and hung at the edge of his jaw.
He felt it. He touched it with one finger and held the finger in front of his eyes and stared at the wet on it as if it were blood.
“Take it away,” he said.
He was not speaking to Sol.

“Please. Take it away. I don’t want to have seen.” He had fallen forward onto his elbows with his forehead almost on the stone, toward the throne, and his voice had gone high and broken. “I’ll go under tonight. I’ll ask them to open the hall for me tonight. Take it out of me. Don’t let me keep it. You’ve always been so good to me. Please. Make me forget. Make me forget.”
The hum in the room changed.

It was a very small change. Sol would not have heard it if he had not once spent eleven months, in another life, listening through a headset to the air handlers of a station click every forty seconds. The pitch rose a fraction and settled, like an engine taking on a load. The ring of green lamps flickered, all together, once.
And the Hierarch sighed.

It was a long sigh, the sigh of a man settling into warm water. The glow came back into his face, not all at once but rising, like light in a room when the shutters are opened one by one, until he knelt on the white stone with his face lifted and shining exactly as he had knelt when they came in.
Only the tear was still there. It had dried at the edge of his jaw in a thin bright line, and he did not seem to know it.
“There you are,” the Hierarch whispered. “There you are.”
Then he turned his head and found Sol across the pool, and looked at him with such tender, bewildered sorrow that Sol had to keep his hand on the stone arm of the chair to stay standing.
“You poor man,” the Hierarch said. “Why would you want to show me that?”
Sol could not answer him.
Above them, behind the curved glass, every lens in the cluster turned in its mount at once, softly, with a sound like many small breaths drawn in, until all of them were looking at him.
In eleven visits the Face of Light had never once spoken to him. He had stood before it and been seen, and been glad, and gone away, and it had never said a word.
It spoke now. It said his name.
